clue.text: Shot can sadly go from can right here?

parts.note: a cut is a stroke played square on the off side in cricket
a can is a tin container

indicators.note: sadly suggests the letters are in a sorry, disordered state and must be rearranged

parts.note: can is slang for a toilet, as is loo

explanation.surface: A film director laments that a shot in the can may end up discarded in the edit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' rearranges GO FROM into GROOMF. The two 'can's give different words, TIN then LOO. 'here' points to the place where unused footage is thrown away, so the whole clue reads as a description of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Footage cut from a film is said, figuratively, to end up on the floor of the editing suite.

clue.text: Arrive at wake

definitions.meaning: to reach a total or a decision, as in 'the bill reaches forty pounds'

explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to reach a figure or conclusion and to recover consciousness.

clue.text: System of notation originally found in different locations

indicators.note: in places the opening letter of the next word within the rearranged letters
different signals that the letters of locations take a different order
originally means only the start of the word found is used

explanation.surface: A scholar describes a musical system first discovered in several separate places.
explanation.walkthrough: 'different' turns LOCATIONS into TONICSOLA, and 'originally' takes F from 'found'; 'in' puts that F inside, before the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a method of writing music using syllables such as doh, ray and me instead of staff notes.

clue.text: Hot on keeping women apart

indicators.note: keeping means holding something within, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: being hot on something means being keen on it, i.e. into it
W is the abbreviation for women, as on toilet doors

explanation.surface: Someone keen on segregating the sexes keeps women separate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeping' puts W inside INTO. The answer is used as in 'broke in two', meaning into separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Something split into two halves has been broken asunder.

clue.text: Breaking points: servicemen blow off about it; I tag manufacturers

indicators.note: breaking means the word is split open, with the rest of the wordplay set inside it

parts.note: gists are the main points of an argument
RAF is the Royal Air Force, so its members are servicemen

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the vulgar word is placed round the next two pieces

parts.note: to blow off is slang for breaking wind
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rowdy scene in which servicemen break wind while someone spray-paints a signature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking' splits the points word after its first letter, and 'about' wraps the slang for breaking wind round 'it' and 'I'. A tag is a graffiti writer's stylised signature.
explanation.definitionFit: Street painters who spray their stylised signature on walls produce what is called a tag.

clue.text: New hero's theme-song involving a somewhat attractive U-shaped bar

indicators.note: involving means taking in, so the article is set within the rearranged letters
new signals the letters of hero's theme-song are made into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A new song about a hero features a mildly appealing curved metal bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges HEROS THEME SONG and 'involving' brings A in among those letters. 'somewhat attractive' is a playful way of saying magnetic.
explanation.definitionFit: A bent bar of iron curved like a shoe for a horse is magnetised to attract metal.

clue.text: Someone diverting fines through work, say

indicators.note: through means one piece passes into the middle of another

parts.note: OP, short for opus, is a musical work
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine, so two of them give FF
to utter something is to say it

explanation.surface: A clerk describes someone who dodges paying fines by doing community work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'through' runs the two fines into the middle of the work. 'diverting' means deterring or putting someone off, not amusing them.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who discourages or deters others is a deterrent figure, turning them away from a course.

clue.text: Artist does picture

parts.note: to do someone is to swindle or con them
table is an old word for a picture painted on a panel or tablet

explanation.surface: An artist produces a painting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'does' is the verb meaning cheats, not a plural noun. John Constable was an English landscape painter.
explanation.definitionFit: John Constable was the English painter of The Hay Wain.

clue.text: Virtually inhumane experiment got up on board these vessels

indicators.note: virtually means almost, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: an inhumane act is a cruel one

indicators.note: got up in a down clue means the word is read from the bottom upward

parts.note: a test is an experiment

explanation.surface: Sailors are horrified by a near-inhumane trial conducted aboard their ships.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Virtually' cuts CRUEL to CRUE and 'got up' turns TEST into TSET. 'board' is a dining table, not a ship's deck.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a stand of condiment containers such as salt, pepper and oil placed on the dining table.

clue.text: See 1 across
Particular target to the west penetrated by slick unit

indicators.note: penetrated by means something else is pushed inside this piece
to the west in an across clue means reading leftward, backwards

parts.note: an aim is a target

indicators.note: slick suggests deft or smart handling, so the letters of unit are reworked

explanation.surface: A specific target in the west is infiltrated by a smooth military unit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to the west' reads the target backwards; 'slick' rearranges UNIT into NUTI; 'penetrated by' pushes NUTI into the reversed word. 'Particular' is a noun here, a detail.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny detail is a small particular point, one of the finer points of something.

clue.text: Ship's spread contributing to unusual feast?

indicators.note: unusual signals these letters appear in an unusual order

parts.note: the possessive gives no extra letter

explanation.surface: A ship's sandwich spread makes an odd contribution to a banquet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' rearranges SHIP and FEAST together.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a savoury paste for spreading on bread, made from fish.

clue.text: Check carpet

definitions.meaning: to mark an item on a list as done
to carpet someone is to scold them

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both marking an item as done on a list and giving someone a reprimand.

clue.text: When one managing trains masters departure time through States borders

parts.note: in can mean through, as in 'in the post'

indicators.note: borders means lies around the edges of, so this verb surrounds the next piece

parts.note: to state something is to say it
ETD is the abbreviation for estimated time of departure

explanation.surface: A railway chief trains masters at the departure time while crossing state borders.
explanation.walkthrough: In the UK, INSET (in-service training) days are school days when the head runs training for teachers, so 'masters' are schoolmasters and 'trains' is a verb, not railway stock.
explanation.definitionFit: These are school days given over to staff training while pupils stay home.

clue.text: Hungry wolf, is it, I see frightening off a clairvoyant?

indicators.note: frightening off means scaring one letter away and letting another take its place

parts.note: a hungry wolf is a predator
I and C together sound like 'I see'

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a hungry wolf is scaring off a fortune-teller.
explanation.walkthrough: IC replaces A in PREDATOR. The question mark marks the definition as loose, since forecasting is not quite the same as second sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A clairvoyant claims to foresee events, so is one who forecasts the future.

clue.text: Message for Clouseau: that is a missing jewel thief, caught short

indicators.note: caught means captured within, so one piece holds the other inside it
missing means the letter named is lost from the French word

parts.note: Inspector Clouseau, the bumbling French detective, would say voilà for 'there it is'
taken as written

indicators.note: short means the word is cut by its final letter

parts.note: iceman is US underworld slang for a diamond thief, ice being diamonds

explanation.surface: A recorded message for Inspector Clouseau reports that a jewel thief has been nabbed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missing' drops the final A of the French word, leaving VOIL; 'short' cuts the thief's last letter, leaving ICEMA; 'caught' holds ICEMA inside, after the first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A recorded phone message left for someone who is unavailable is stored this way.

clue.text: Brilliant opening, defending powerful man up on trial

indicators.note: defending means guarding something by surrounding it, so these pieces enclose the others

parts.note: an ace is someone brilliant at something
the rook is one of the most powerful men on a chessboard
to be up on something is to be in on it, informed about it
a slot is an opening

explanation.surface: A brilliant start to the defence of a mighty figure on trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'defending' wraps the brilliant word and the opening round the chess piece and 'up on', the split falling after the first letter. The phrase is old-fashioned: a hardship in one's life.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic idiom means an affliction or hardship that a person must bear.

clue.text: I put in stake for poker game, initially cordial

indicators.note: in places the first two pieces inside the poker stake

parts.note: the ante is the stake each player puts in at the start of a poker hand
to set something down is to put it there

explanation.surface: A gambler stakes money on a poker game, starting with a friendly gesture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' belongs to the stake: the ante is paid at the start of a hand. 'cordial' is the noun for a sweet liqueur, not the adjective for friendly.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a sweet aniseed-flavoured liqueur, a kind of drink also called a cordial.

clue.text: An absence of Christmas spirit? It's not seemly

parts.note: Christmas falls in December, abbreviated Dec
O, zero, represents nothing, an absence
rum is an alcoholic spirit

explanation.surface: A lack of festive cheer is considered improper.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a gloomy Christmas, but 'Christmas' gives IN DEC because Christmas falls in December.
explanation.definitionFit: Unseemly conduct is a lapse of propriety, behaviour that breaks good manners.

clue.text: Plant with beautiful leaves blooming termly

indicators.note: blooming suggests the letters open out like flowers into a new shape

explanation.surface: A plant whose lovely foliage flowers once every school term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blooming' rearranges TERMLY.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an evergreen shrub with glossy aromatic leaves and white flowers.

clue.text: Brother's welcomed home following a pardon

indicators.note: following means this part comes after the single letter
welcomed means taken in, so the exclamation encloses the next piece

parts.note: 'Brother!' and 'My!' are both exclamations of surprise; the 's means has
a nest is a home

explanation.surface: A monk returns home after receiving a pardon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brother' is an exclamation of surprise, not a sibling or monk; 'welcomed' puts home inside it, and 'following' sets all that after A.
explanation.definitionFit: An official pardon is a general forgiveness granted to offenders.

clue.text: It helps to make jelly start to wobble at the top

indicators.note: to wobble at the top means the opening letters of the word shift about

parts.note: an intro is the start of something, such as a song

explanation.surface: Something helps a jelly to set, but it wobbles at the top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to wobble at the top' swaps the first two letters of INTRO. 'jelly' is slang for gelignite, made with nitroglycerine, not a pudding.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitroglycerine is a key ingredient of gelignite, known as jelly.

clue.text: See 2
Engineer rings about redcap in pursuit of bivouacker

indicators.note: rings means surrounds, so the engineer encloses the pieces that follow

parts.note: CA, short for circa, means about
a redcap is a military policeman, MP

explanation.surface: An engineer surrounds a military policeman who is chasing a camper.
explanation.walkthrough: A redcap is a British military policeman, named after the red cover on the cap; 'rings' sets him, with 'about' and 'in', inside the engineer.
explanation.definitionFit: Setting up a temporary camp is what someone sleeping out in a bivouac does.

clue.text: A brief communication on this, available to rent online?

definitions.text: A brief communication on this, available to rent online?

parts.words: A brief communication on this, available to rent online?
parts.note: a short folded card for a short message; read as '...', a property not yet let on the internet and so still for rent

explanation.definitionFit: It is a small folded sheet of writing paper for short messages.

clue.text: Having let it loose, tools put away — door of empty stable now secured!

definitions.text: door of empty stable now secured!

indicators.note: having means containing, so the pair of implements hold the next piece

parts.note: two tools give the word tool twice

indicators.note: loose signals the letters of let it are set free and rearranged

parts.note: to put food away is to eat it

explanation.surface: A stable owner, having let the horse loose and stored the tools, finally locks the empty stable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loose' rearranges LET IT into ITTLE, which 'Having' sets between the two TOOLs. Locking the stable door after the horse has bolted is the proverbial action that comes after the damage is done.
explanation.definitionFit: Locking a stable door once the horse has bolted is the classic example of an inadequate, belated response.
